case.case_title: Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports [1984] 2 Sri L.R.

clause.text: General restrictions may apply for national security, public order, health, morality, and welfare.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the banning of the Saturday Review newspaper by the Competent Authority under Emergency Regulations was justified under the restrictions allowed by Article 15(7) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners argued that the banning of the Saturday Review violated their fundamental rights to equality and freedom of speech and expression, and that there was no justification for the orders under the Emergency Regulations.
case_context.respondent_argument: The Competent Authority contended that the ban was necessary for national security and public order, based on material published in the Saturday Review that was prejudicial to these interests, and that the orders were made in good faith and within the bounds of reasonableness.
key_facts: The Saturday Review was banned repeatedly under Regulation 14(3) of the Emergency (Miscellaneous Provisions and Powers) Regulations during a declared State of Emergency.
The newspaper was published in Jaffna, an area with considerable disorder and threat to national security at the time.
The Competent Authority formed the opinion that the newspaper's content encouraged violence and communal disharmony.
The petitioners were readers and contributors claiming violation of their rights due to the ban.
The Court had to consider the reasonableness of the Competent Authority's discretion under emergency conditions.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that the fundamental rights, including freedom of speech and expression, are subject to restrictions prescribed by law for national security, public order, and other interests as enumerated in Article 15(7). The Competent Authority's discretion under the Emergency Regulations must be exercised reasonably and in good faith. The Court will not substitute its own opinion if the Competent Authority's decision is within reasonable bounds, especially during a State of Emergency.
reasoning.application_to_facts: Given the material published in the Saturday Review and the context of the emergency and unrest in Jaffna, the Court found that the Competent Authority's opinion and consequent ban were not unreasonable. The restrictions imposed were lawful under Article 15(7) as they aimed to preserve public order and national security.
principles_established: Fundamental rights can be restricted under Article 15(7) for national security and public order.
The Court's review of emergency orders is limited to assessing reasonableness, not substituting its own judgment.
Discretion exercised in good faith by the Competent Authority during emergencies is given deference.
The freedom of speech and expression includes the freedom of the recipient but is subject to the same restrictions.
precedents_cited: Secretary of State for Education & Science v. Tameside Metropolitan Borough Council [1976] 3 WLR 652
AG of St. Christopher v. Reynolds [1979] 3 All E.R. 129 (P.C.)

outcome.holding: The Court upheld the Competent Authority's orders banning the Saturday Review as lawful restrictions under Article 15(7). The petitioners' claims under Article 14(1)(a) and Article 12(1) failed as the restrictions were justified and reasonable.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 15(7) provides the constitutional basis for lawful restrictions on fundamental rights during emergencies for national security and public order, which was central to the Court's reasoning and ultimate dismissal of the petitioners' claims.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court found that the Competent Authority acted within the bounds of reasonableness under Article 15(7) given the material published in the Saturday Review and the emergency context, and thus the fundamental rights were lawfully restricted.
